newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian election two years away - Howard.
newsitem.headline: Australian election two years away - Howard.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Wednesday an election was two years away, contrasting with his remark last month that it would be held in 15 to 18 months.
"We're two years away from an election," Howard told Melbourne radio 3AW, when asked about the strategy his Liberal-National coalition would adopt.
Constitutionally, an election for the House of Representatives and Senate must be held no later than the first half of 1999, although Howard can practically hold it in the second half of 1998.

Howard was non-committal on whether the coalition would lend mutual election support to the One Nation party of controversial MP Pauline Hanson, who opposes Asian immigration, Aboriginal welfare and economic reform.
Australia's preferential voting system seeks to return consensus candidates by redistributing the votes of low-polling candidates according to voters' numbered preferences.

Two parties can maximise each other's chances by encouraging their supporters to give their second-preference to the other party. So if one of them is eliminated for want of support, the other gets the vote.
But when asked whether his party would have such a deal with One Nation, Howard disowned responsibility and said the decision was up to his party head office.
"This is a matter that will be decided by the Liberal Party organisation," he said.
"We'll decide how to allocate preferences when we get closer to the election."

Howard is under considerable political pressure from Hanson, who has gained about 10 percent voter support in recent months, mostly at the expense of the Liberal Party and its National Party coalition partner.
The Labor Opposition, seeking to associate Howard with Hanson policies that most Australians reject, has pressured him to say whether there would be a preference swap.
